name: Esther Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Esther, 27, and I'm a junior buyer at Oakfield Building Supplies. We're a builders' merchant: timber, plasterboard, cement, insulation, sold to builders and to the big DIY shops. I live with my partner Tom, who runs his own plumbing business with one van. I left school at 18, worked in the yard for a year, then got into the buying office.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First thing I check the timber prices, because they move every week, and I look at what the branches sold yesterday. I place orders with the sawmills and the plasterboard makers, and my boss Graham checks anything over a certain amount. I sometimes use an AI chat tool to check my sums or write a polite chasing email. I like it when a lorry of timber turns up on time and the yard lads cheer. I hate the weeks when the price of insulation jumps and I've already quoted the builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise for a better calculator. At work I'd say we were right not to spend a fortune on it. Online I'd keep quiet; I don't argue with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine with it. I'd keep using the chat tool now and then and keep learning the trade the slow way. My job's about knowing the sawmills, and that still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and ask Graham to let me handle the insulation range myself. Tom and I would keep saving; we've got about eight months put away, plus his van's paid off. We'd probably start looking at houses next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the normal path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest worry in your job right now, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Builders going bust, mostly. Last winter one of our big customers went under owing us money, and it was a nightmare for weeks. That kind of thing is what actually keeps me up, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Tom's work steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, Tom's always busy. People's boilers break whether AI is clever or not.

steps.text: Ask Graham to hand over the insulation range
Start house-hunting with Tom next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to use the tools, but bosses should be fair about it. At work I'd want to know the plan before rumours start. I'd ask Graham straight out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying is right there on that list, and I'm the junior. If the software can place the sawmill orders, my boss Graham keeps the senior buyers and maybe one junior. I'd want to be that one, but I'm not the best at it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the training if Oakfield brings in AI ordering, and I'd be the first to sign up, not the last. I'd also talk to Tom about doing his quotes and books, because he hates that side. We'd hold off on the house for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but there's a knot there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doing Tom's books sounds like a fallback. Would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd be giving up something I worked for. But Tom's business is growing and he needs someone on the office side, so it's not a step down, just sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change with the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We'd keep the savings for now and see. If my job's still there in a year, we buy then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs slowing down, and that companies shouldn't be allowed to sack everyone at once. I'd vote for whoever promised a sensible transition. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my buying job's gone by 2028, no question. Ordering timber is thinking work. Tom's plumbing is safe till the robots come around 2031. For three years, my partner Tom's plumbing van is our only income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Oakfield before they let me go, maybe within the year, and join Tom properly. I'd do his office and learn to fit bathrooms with him, so there are two pairs of hands. We'd cut back hard and keep the eight months of savings as our backstop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My job's going and Tom's only lasts a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031, when robots can do plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're both stuck, and I don't know. Maybe people would still want a person in their house, not a robot. That's what I'd hope, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No house. No holidays. We'd still go to my parents for Sunday dinner, because that's free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's plan. At work I'd ask what Oakfield's doing for staff. I'd tell friends to get a trade if they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my buying job goes around 2031. But I'd have time to build up Tom's business with him first. By 2031 we could have two vans and a proper bathroom-fitting side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Oakfield for two more years and keep saving. I'd do a part-time course in bathroom fitting from next year. Around 2028 I'd join Tom full time, and we'd buy a second van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting your savings into Tom's business means both of you depend on one thing. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's a risk. Plumbing and bathrooms need hands for longer than buying does, and I'd rather bet on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy a smaller house in 2027, before it all changes. A home's the thing I'd want sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up and people should use it. I'd say the same at Oakfield: no excuses. Online I'd still keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be all right. I'd be 37, with ten years to move into Tom's business at our own pace. Hands-on work lasts till 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying for five years and get good at it. Tom and I would buy a house next year. I'd learn the AI ordering tools as they come, and around 2030 I'd start moving to the van side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the AI tools here but not leave yet. Is that a balance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's my centre bit. Use the tools while they help you, and don't fall in love with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk for you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Ten years goes fast, and if I'm still buying timber in 2035 I've left it late.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job goes, and Tom's only has three years left, and that's too short to build anything. What would help is help for small trade businesses, like cheap loans or training grants, so families like ours can adapt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the builders. If building gets cheaper because of robots, maybe more houses get built, and that's one good bit I'd like to see.

headlineQuote: If building gets cheaper because of robots, maybe more houses get built, and that's one good bit I'd like to see.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** junior buyer at Oakfield, a builders' merchant.
She lives with Tom, a self-employed **plumber**, and they have eight months saved.
She's pragmatic and uses AI **now and then**, learning tools once proven.
In faster scenarios she'd **join Tom's business**, betting on hands-on work.
She blames nobody in particular and backs a **sensible transition**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job goes and Tom's trade has only three years left.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** and **training grants** for small trade businesses.
